summary_sentence: For example, on June 21 the Sun rises over New York at azimuth 58.3° — well north of east — and sets at 301.7°, which is why summer evenings light north-facing windows.

Computed sunrise azimuth: 58.3° on June 21, 90.6° at the March equinox, 121.6° on December 21 — a 63° sweep along the horizon across the year. 'The Sun rises in the east' is the equinox-only truth.

faq: What is azimuth, in plain words?
The compass direction of the Sun, measured clockwise from north: 90° is an eastern Sun, 180° southern, 270° western.
From north on this site — the modern standard. Some older solar texts use south; mixing them flips your answer by 180°.
The Sun's declination leans the rise point north or south of east except at the equinoxes. Latitude widens the lean.
In the tropics the noon Sun can stand north (azimuth near 0°) on some dates — the formula handles it; intuition from temperate zones does not.
Add or subtract local magnetic declination (the True North vs Magnetic tool covers it) — in parts of the US the gap exceeds 15°.
A small fraction of a degree from the standard solar algorithm — tighter than any compass you will hold.
At the pole every direction is south (or north) and azimuth becomes the Sun's hour angle in disguise — the calculator still reports the formal value.
